title: TB2-13939
frame:
Forum: Refugee Protection Division (first-instance tribunal).
Parties: the claimant and the Minister; names are redacted.
Decision under review: none; this is the first-instance decision.
How the layers nest here: The member of the tribunal is the author (layer 1). The claimant and the Minister make submissions to the member (layer 2). There is no earlier decision-maker unless the reasons describe a prior decision (layer 3). Testimony and documents are layer 5.

paragraphs.text: XXXX XXXX, the claimant, is a citizen of the People's Republic of China (China). He claims refugee protection pursuant to section 96 and subsections 97(1)(a) and (b) of the Immigration and Refugee Protection Act1(IRPA).

The claimant alleges he developed back pain associated with his work abroad in construction. His friend seeing his discomfort approached him in XXXX 2011 and explained that Falun Gong could help his problems. The claimant decided he would learn the exercises associated with Falun Gong and joined his friend's Falun Gong practice group in XXXX 2012. He became a regular attending member. The Public Security Bureau (PSB) discovered this group on XXXX XXXX, 2012. He escaped and went into hiding. The PSB subsequently went to his family's home in search of the claimant. The claimant felt he could not remain in the country safely and sought the assistance of a smuggler to leave the country. He arrived in Canada on XXXX XXXX, 2012 and made a claim for refugee protection on October 26, 2012.
For the reasons that follow, the panel finds that the claimant is neither a Convention refugee nor a person in need of protection. ANALYSIS Identity

The claimant's testimony and the supporting documentation filed,2 his Resident Identity Card (RIC), Household Register (hukou) and Marriage Certificate, establish the claimant's identity as a national of China. Credibility

One of the determinative issues in this claim is the credibility of the claimant's Personal Information Form (PIF)3 narrative and oral testimony concerning the claimant's membership in the Falun Gong discipline and his pursuit by agents of the PSB. The panel finds that the claimant was not a credible witness in this regard and is not currently wanted for arrest by the PSB on account of Falun Gong activities in China. As well, the panel finds that should he return to China, there is not a serious possibility that he would be persecuted. The reasons for this decision are noted below.

In assessing credibility, the panel was mindful of the claimant's age, education, and background. He alleges that he has nine years of education. In addition, the panel is cognizant of the many difficulties faced by a claimant in establishing a claim, including cultural factors, the milieu of the hearing room, and the stress inherent in responding to oral questions through an interpreter. The panel has taken these considerations into account in arriving at negative credibility findings. The Public Security Bureau (PSB) visit

The panel inquired how many times the PSB had come to his home in China in search of the claimant up to the day prior to his refugee hearing. He replied, "I think it's at least twenty times". The claimant was asked if the PSB had left a summons or warrant with his family indicating their interest in him. The claimant said "Yes". The panel notes that country condition documents4 indicate that a summons is often left with or shown to family members when the police want someone to come to their headquarters. In addition, the summons is the documentary basis for the subsequent issuance of an arrest warrant if the person in whom they are interested does not respond to the summons. The panel queried as to whether the claimant appeared for the summons. He answered, "No". The claimant was asked if a warrant had been issued because he did not respond to the summons. He responded in the negative. Although this policy is not always implemented, it is reasonable to believe from the PSB actions of allegedly issuing a summons that a subsequent document would have been issued in respect of the claimant given that the claimant's statements indicate the PSB have an interest in following procedure.

Although the documentary evidence is mixed, it is reasonable to conclude that the authorities have concluded some investigation which gives rise to them stating that he was identified as a Falun Gong participant. Further, given that the authorities have allegedly continued to inquire about the claimant, it is reasonable to expect, given the documentary evidence that an arrest warrant would also have been left with the claimant's family.

He was next asked if the PSB said anything else to his family on any of the visits beyond what had been related in his PIF and testimony about the PSB's first two visits. He replied "No" and confirmed it was similar each time. The panel recognizing that repeated visits could be upsetting for the claimant's family inquired if other than that was his family living safely and well in China at this time. He answered, "Yes".

To have allegedly attended his family home on over twenty occasions over the course of two and a half years would indicate that the PSB had far more than a casual interest in the claimant. The absence of a warrant when one should reasonably have been issued damages the credibility of the claimant. As well it is reasonable to believe that the PSB may be frustrated in having attended his family home numerous times and become more aggressive in their action to influence his family to convince the claimant to surrender.

This causes one to question the activities of the PSB. The actions (or lack thereof) indicated by the claimant run counter to conventional beliefs that the PSB are a ruthless and fearsome police force. The claimant's testimony runs counter to documentary evidence about the PSB's methods and is found not to be credible.

The panel is of the view, that considering the analysis of documentary evidence in respect of Falun Gong practitioners in China, the claimant's testimony that the PSB came to his home between XXXX 2012 and XXXX 2015 twenty or more times to ask about him, but taking no additional action, thereby wasting their valuable time and resources, is singularly implausible and further detracts from his credibility. The Claimant's Family in China

The claimant did not adduce any evidence that his family in China has suffered any consequences as a result of his participation in Falun Gong and failure to surrender to the police. Country documentary evidence5 regarding Falun Gong states that it is considered a cult by the Chinese government and is banned, and indicates that Chinese authorities use the family of absconding practitioners as hostages to force the practitioner to give up the practice. If a practitioner does not cooperate with the authorities, the family is subject to punishment as well, including harassment, arbitrary interrogation, losing a job, and losing housing benefits. In the context of this case, where the absconding person has not returned for nearly two years, and as alleged by the claimant, the PSB are still looking for him, it is reasonable to assume that his family would have experienced all or some of the punishments noted above. The claimant alleges that his family was only warned not to conceal information on the whereabouts of the claimant and warned that they would suffer consequences if they were found to assisting him in any way. The panel draws a negative inference from the claimant's family continuing ability to carry on with their normal life without facing consequences at the hands of the PSB. The Summons

The claimant entered a document entitled, "Notice of Summoning",6 that he alleged was left at his family home by the PSB. The claimant noted this document was delivered on the second PSB visit. As indicated previously, the documentary evidence7 regarding the issuance of a summons notes that a summons would almost always be issued to the individual rather than a household or family member. However, it is also noted that it is very common in China for the police authorities to leave the summons with family members, instructing them to pass it along to the person named on the summons. The person accepting the summons would be expected to sign an acknowledgment of receipt.

As discussed previously the panel has credibility concerns around the issuing of the subpoena and actions of the PSB. The claimant in his testimony stated that this was proof that the PSB were seeking to arrest him. The panel notes that the claimant through his oral testimony and statements in his PIF has indicated he is not adverse to obtaining and utilizing fraudulent documents. The claimant at question 15 in the PIF states he utilized an "improperly obtained" Canadian visa to exit China and travel to Canada. The panel is led to conclude that the claimant has the means and ability to secure duplicitous documentation to assist in his quest for refugee protection in Canada.

Documentary evidence8 indicates fraudulent documents are readily available to Chinese refugee claimants: An official at the Canadian embassy in Beijing wrote that there are "consistent reports" of document fraud in China and that fraudulent identity documents (IDs) are easily obtained in the country. Similarly, a professor of criminal justice at Xavier University who specializes in Chinese policing stated in correspondence with the Research Directorate that "[t]here is little question that fraud of all kind[s], including ID fraud, is a major problem in China". The Professor added that fraudulent IDs are "easily accessible" and that the industry is a "big business" and an "open secret" in China. In July 2012, the state media source China.org.cn described the fraudulent ID industry as "an incredibly lucrative trade," ... According to the Beijing embassy official, the provinces of Guangdong and Fujian are "considered particularly high-risk for fraudulent documents".
The panel in reviewing and assessing the genuineness of the claimant's document notes it is not produced with any known security features and is printed on plain stock.

The Federal Court of Appeal held in Orelien9 that "[O]ne cannot be satisfied that the evidence is credible or trustworthy, unless satisfied that it is probably so, not just possibly so." Therefore, findings of fact, as well as the determination as to whether the claimant's evidence is credible, are made on a balance of probabilities. A witness' testimony does not have to be accepted simply because it was not contradicted at the hearing. The Refugee Protection Division is entitled to make reasonable findings based on implausibility, common sense and rationality, and may reject evidence if it is not consistent with the probabilities affecting the case as a whole.10

The panel has considered the claimant's testimony, the inconsistency in the actions of the PSB, as well as the ease with which one can get fraudulent documents in China. The panel has cause to question the genuineness of the document and places little weight on the summons submitted as support for this claim. Prison Visiting Card

The claimant submitted a "Prison Visiting Card" document11 in support of his claim for refugee protection. The panel in assessing the genuineness of the information notes that this document is a faxed copy or photocopy of the document and not an original. The panel is not able to verify what type of stock it is printed on, nor able to ascertain whether the document was produced with known security features. The copy does not allow a clear review of the contents or the photograph of the document. The panel indicated that the document bears a stamp. However, the panel noted it appears that information is written over the stamp although without the original, the panel is unable to confirm one way or the other. Further to this the panel noted for the claimant that the seal was not continuous, displaying breaks at the edge of the photograph. The purpose of a stamp is to "seal" the document to attest to its genuineness and as a means to demonstrate that it has not been altered or tampered with. The presence of data written over a seal undermines the integrity of the stamp and as a result, the credibility of the document itself.

The panel has previously discussed that documentary evidence12 indicates fraudulent documents are readily available to Chinese refugee claimants. Additionally the panel has addressed that that the claimant is not adverse to obtaining and utilizing fraudulent documents in pursuit of refugee protection in Canada.

The panel further inquired if the claimant in speaking with his introducer's family if he had considered inquiring if it was possible to obtain copies of an arrest warrant, court sentencing or detention documents to assist in supporting his claim for refugee protection. He answered in the negative.

With this information in its mind, considering the facts and documentary evidence surrounding the claimant's document presented in evidence, the panel places little evidentiary weight on the Inmate's Visiting Card presented as support in this claim.

It was apparent as discussed above that there were a number of important credibility concerns regarding the claimant's testimony and documents alleging his ongoing pursuit be the PSB in China. The panel finds on a balance of probabilities that the claimant is not facing arrest at the hands of the PSB.

This leads the panel to question the overall credibility of the claimant in presenting his claim for refugee protection. When assessing the findings herein, the panel finds on a balance of probabilities that the claimant has failed to act as credible witness. Falun Gong Identity

The panel asked the claimant if he was familiar with Zhuan Falun, the principal text associated with the Falun Gong discipline. He stated that he was and "had read it briefly". He explained that he "does not study the Fa (the philosophy associated with Falun Gong as described in the text Zhuan Falun) regularly as I have low education". He added, "I do it every week if I have spare time".

The panel notes, the comments of Master Li (the founder of Falun Gong); "Why do I tell you to study, read, and memorize Zhuan Falun? To guide your cultivation! As to those who only do the exercises but don't study the Fa, they are not disciples of Dafa whatsoever.13

The panel has considered the claimant's comments in respect of his "low education" and finds that his nine years of education does not exclude him regular study and mastery of Zhuan Falun at a level commensurate with his education. The panel further asked the claimant to describe an average week of activities as a Falun Gong practitioner. He described that he read the "book" every Wednesday evening, he attended group practice Saturday and Sunday and that he goes to "learn the law (philosophy) Wednesday. The claimant was further questioned as to whether he performed the exercises on a daily basis. He replied, "No, I just send out "Righteous Thoughts". The panel finds the claimant's description of his actions in Canada in respect of his adherence to the philosophy and lifestyle of a Falun Gong practitioner is inconsistent with the values set out by Master Li.

The panel queried as to whether the claimant could compare the similarities in the practice of Falun Gong in China and Canada. The claimant replied, "the five exercises, Falun Dafa, Righteous Thoughts".

The panel reviewed the claimant's statement in an attempt to clarify his response. The panel confirmed the exercises that make up the Falun Gong practice system were similar as well as the action of putting forward Righteous Thoughts.

The panel refocused the question and the claimant appeared to be struggling to provide additional input. The panel assisted him by asking if he practiced in a group setting in China. He answered, "Yes". The panel confirmed the claimant practiced in a group setting in Canada. He was next asked if his group practiced with a leader in China and the panel confirmed the same was true in Canada. The claimant was subsequently questioned whether he practiced the exercises at home in China as well as in Canada. He answered in the affirmative and agreed this would be another similarity. The panel having clarified the question for the claimant expected that this might lead to spontaneous input from the claimant. The panel inquired if he understood the question and asked if so, could he point out any other similarities. He was unable to provide any additional input.

The panel carried on to query as to whether the claimant's group played music in China and in Canada. He confirmed this was correct. The panel again confirmed this would be a similarity in practice. The panel inquired if the claimant studied the philosophy associated with Falun Gong in China and in Canada. He confirmed that he did study "the Law" in both countries and this would also be a similarity in practice. The claimant was asked if he conducted his life as a Falun Gong practitioner in accordance with a specific motto or philosophy in China. He stated that he did and indicated it was "Truth, Compassion and Forbearance". The panel again confirmed that he conducted his life the same way in Canada.

The claimant was questioned as to why he required prompting from the panel to provide responses. He replied, "I am nervous". The panel rejects this response noting it was utilized throughout the hearing when the claimant was unable to provide a response to questions put to him. The claimant was able to testify with confidence and without hesitation when providing details contained in his Personal Information Form. The only time he expressed that he was nervous was when he was unable to provide responses to direct questions. The panel noted for the claimant they had provided examples of what types of responses were being sought and that the question had been rephrased for the claimant. The panel having prompted the claimant and clarified the question finds it reasonable to expect that the claimant could spontaneously identify simple common aspects of his practice of Falun Gong, especially considering many of these concepts were identified in the claimant's PIF narrative.

The panel noted for the claimant that he had indicated that he lived his life as a Falun Gong practitioner in China utilizing the concept of "Truth" and asked if this was the same in Canada. He answered, "No", stating that he was unable to spread the "Truth", in China. The panel explained that his PIF narrative described that his friend introduced him to Falun Gong, explaining the benefits, how it helped him and could help the claimant. The panel inquired if this was the action of spreading the "Truth". The claimant then modified his testimony to confirm that he would spread the "Truth" to others in China. The claimant's lack of awareness as indicated in his testimony leads the panel to draw a negative inference to his credibility and leads the panel to conclude on a balance of probabilities that the claimant has not practiced Falun Gong in China. Further to this conclusion, the panel has cause to question the claimant's participation in Falun Gong practice in Canada.

The panel asked the claimant if he could provide specific examples of how he utilized the concept of "Truth" to his daily life as a Falun Gong practitioner in Canada. He proceeded to describe being "in a line-up for a bus and someone pushed ahead in the line. He next explained that he would not be angry with this action". The panel noted that this would be an example of the concept of "Forbearance" and asked if there were any examples that might be specific to his situation. The claimant attempted to restate his initial example, noting that he "Tries to tell them the truth and do good things" but he struggled to respond. The panel drew his attention to a photograph submitted with his personal disclosure14 where he was depicted holding a banner at a Falun Gong event. The panel questioned as to whether this would be an example of the claimant promoting the "Truth" in Canada. He confirmed this was correct. The claimant was subsequently asked why when he had submitted this documentation; he would require prompting to explain its application. He responded, "I did not remember to say that". The panel finds this response makes little sense. The panel has considered that an individual who has adopted a lifestyle and a philosophy based on seminal events in his life, should not need to "remember to say that". The panel finds on a balance of probabilities that the claimant's presence in these photographs indicates the claimant's attempt to foster an association with activities, which he knows little about, but senses his appearance in these activities will somehow bolster his claim. The panel draws a negative inference to the credibility of the claimant's identity as a Falun Gong practitioner.

The panel further noted for the claimant that his PIF narrative stated that a friend had encouraged the claimant to become a Falun Gong practitioner because of health concerns. The panel asked if the claimant could provide any other reasons other than health concerns to identify why an individual might practice Falun Gong. He answered, "Because people get sick". The panel rephrased the question and he replied, "The other thing is karma".

The panel notes the claimant appears to have learned a series of responses or facts associated with Falun Gong that he attempts to insert at appropriate locations in testimony. When not confronted with these opportunities, the claimant is often unable to reply. The claimant's response is an example of a situation such as this. The panel carried on to provide some examples of the response it was seeking such as an individual having issues with "anger, the death of someone close to them or conflicts with colleagues at work". The claimant further replied that these are "attachments and you (need) to let go jealousy", which does not address the question put to the claimant.

The panel recognizing that the claimant was struggling to respond and recognizing that health concerns caused him to become a practitioner inquired as to where in the text Zhuan Falun did Master Li discuss the concept of health. The claimant replied, "In Talk Six" (the panel notes the principle text associated with the practice of Falun Gong, Zhuan Falun is divided into nine "talks" or chapters". The panel explained that this was not correct and noted that Master Li discusses "health" in the first few pages of Talk One as well as in Talk Seven. The claimant replied, "Talk Seven discusses topics like on Killing and Eating Meat". The panel finds this is another example of the claimant having learned a few facts such as the topics covered in certain "Talks", but being unable to provide appropriate responses. The panel subsequently queried as to what Master Li states in Talk One that an individual requires in becoming healthy. He answered, "To focus on cultivation". The panel described that Master Li notes, "one must return to their original true self and cultivate". The claimant was asked if he had heard this statement previously and he confirmed the leader had told him this.

The panel notes the claimant has nine years of education, As well he testified to having read the primary text associated with Falun Gong, Zhuan Falun and he continues to read it on a weekly basis. One would realistically expect the claimant to have a reasonable working knowledge of the contents of this text and some of its applications to his chosen lifestyle, even if he did not understand all of its substance. The claimant may have learned the exercises associated with the practice of Falun Gong. The performance of these exercises in and of themselves is not illegal.

The panel further finds that the practice of these exercises is simply analogous to the practice of Qigong, an ancient Chinese form of training for mental and physical health and as Master Li the founder of Falun Gong has indicated, does not define that individual as a genuine Falun Gong practitioner.

In the same context the claimant provided photographs of Falun Gong activities as well as letters15 from alleged Falun Gong practitioners. The activities depicted in the photographs are available to any individual to attend and indicate attendance on the date of the photograph, but they do not address the motivation of the claimant. The panel further notes the photographs were taken on two dates in 2014, long after his 2012 claim for refugee protection. The panel has discussed the claimant's inability to understand and relate aspects of the photographs to his practice of Falun Gong.

The letters attest to practicing with a group of individuals, but do not define what allegedly makes them Falun Gong members. In considering the claimant's limited knowledge and command of the philosophy associated with Falun Gong the panel concludes the claimant's presence in these photographs is simply an attempt to foster an association with Falun Gong.

He was questioned about similarities between the practice of Falun Gong in China and in Canada and he initially identified two basic items, yet when further prompted as to what the panel was seeking, he struggled to provide any additional similarities, many of which were associated with the activities depicted in his narrative and the photographs submitted in evidence.

Through prompting by his counsel, the claimant identified himself in a group sitting outside the Chinese Consulate in Toronto. He was asked if actions such as this concerned him in any way and he replied in the negative. His counsel submits that the claimant is at risk of being identified by the Chinese government. The panel has considered the submissions of counsel and reviewed the documentation.16 The panel notes the document states, "The Toronto FDAC Vice-President stated that Falun Gong practitioners in Canada have been approached by representatives of the Chinese authorities, who threaten their family members in China if they do not stop "criticizing China"."

The claimant when questioned about the experiences of his family members in China following his alleged pursuit by the PSB reported that they were living safely and well. The panel finds there was no persuasive evidence adduced at the hearing to indicate the claimant's risk of harm through these actions has increased and finds counsel's statements are based in speculation.

The panel has stated previously that that a failure to understand the philosophies of Falun Gong makes practicing Falun Gong exercises no more beneficial than practicing any other Qigong exercises. Considering the previous findings, the panel places little weight on these items.

Given the claimant's failure to demonstrate an understanding of the exercises, principles and philosophies associated with Falun Gong and relate some of the key concepts in Zhuan Falun, the panel finds that the claimant has not studied Zhuan Falun nor does he apply the philosophy associated with Falun Gong to his daily life and is therefore not a genuine Falun Gong practitioner. The panel draws a negative inference from the claimant's limited knowledge of Falun Gong and his action of attaching very little significance to understanding and embracing the philosophy of Falun Gong. These findings taken collectively cause the panel to find on a balance of probabilities that the claimant is not a member of the Falun Gong discipline. Any knowledge that the claimant has learned about Falun Gong could easily have been acquired in Canada, in order to advance a fraudulent refugee claim.

If as the panel concludes the claimant is not a genuine Falun Gong practitioner, it follows that the PSB would have no interest in pursuing the claimant for his association with Falun Gong activities in China. Summary

In summary, the panel in assessing a number of the credibility issues surrounding this claim concludes on a balance of probabilities that the claimant has not acted as a credible witness in his quest for refugee protection. In addition, he is not being sought by the PSB for association with the practice of Falun Gong in China. The panel has also found on a balance of probabilities that the claimant is not a genuine Falun Gong practitioner. The panel has further determined on a balance of probabilities that the PSB are not pursuing the claimant for his association with the Falun Gong discipline in China.

The panel has considered all three protection grounds under section 96 and sub-section 97(1) of the Immigration and Refugee Protection Act and, on the basis of the totality of all the evidence made available to the panel, it finds that the claimant has not satisfied his burden of establishing a serious possibility that he would be persecuted in China, nor that he would be subjected personally to a risk to his life or a risk of cruel and unusual treatment or punishment, or to a danger of torture.

For these reasons, the Refugee Protection Division finds that the claimant is not a Convention refugee or a person in need of protection; the claim is rejected. (signed) " R.J. Bebbington " R.J.
